content: Abdominal decompression was originally developed as a method to alleviate pain during labor. It has also been applied in cases of pregnancy complications and in healthy pregnant women with the aim of enhancing fetal well-being and intellectual development. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of prophylactic abdominal decompression on various pregnancy outcomes, including the risk of admission for pre-eclampsia, fetal growth, perinatal morbidity and mortality, and childhood development. A search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register on February 2, 2012, to identify relevant studies. The review included randomized trials that compared abdominal decompression with either a placebo (dummy decompression) or no treatment in healthy pregnant women. Both authors of the review independently assessed the eligibility of the studies and evaluated their methodological quality. Three studies met the inclusion criteria. The results showed no significant differences between the groups that underwent abdominal decompression and the control groups in terms of low birthweight (risk ratio [RR] 0.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.27 to 1.77) or perinatal mortality (RR 2.47, 95% CI 0.77 to 7.92). Additionally, there were no observed differences in the rates of admission for pre-eclampsia, Apgar scores, or measures of childhood development. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the use of abdominal decompression in normal pregnancies. They recommended that future research should focus on the potential applications of abdominal decompression during labor and in pregnancies complicated by medical or obstetric conditions.
